1.0 Context¶

1.1 Situation¶

Our credit card company operates in Taiwan's competitive consumer finance market. Over the past fiscal year, we have observed default rates climbing beyond our expected tolerance threshold for this market. This increase translates to significant unplanned financial losses and threatens our profitability.

Currently, our risk assessment for long term customers relies on a rule-based system developed in 2001 that primarily considers income verification and employment status at the time of application for our credit services. This legacy system focuses only on data known at contract start and fails to incorporate behavioral signals from ongoing account activity—particularly payment patterns that often influence default likelyhood.

Management has approved a series of feasibility studies to evaluate whether machine learning can improve our default risk prediction capabilities using the rich behavioral data we already collect (among others payment history, bill amounts, and repayment behavior). To make sure no insights about the default prediction quality via machine learning algorythms are missed, we start with the earliest data that we have some behavioural features archived for: 2005.

1.2 Value¶

Accurate default prediction creates value through two mechanisms:

Loss Prevention: If we detect a customer that is likely to default we can limit financial damage through proactive interventions such as credit limit reductions, payment plan offers, or increased monitoring.

Operational Efficiency: Our current manual review process flags a high amount of customers for human analyst review. A well-calibrated ML model could reduce this to customers with genuinely elevated risk, freeing analyst capacity for higher-value activities.

Regulatory Compliance: Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission increasingly requires documented, auditable risk assessment processes. Unlike black-box deep learning approaches, the interpretable ML models we evaluate (Decision Trees, K-Nearest Neighbors) can provide clear explanations for credit decisions—essential for regulatory reporting and customer communication.

(see resources 1 to see where this screenshot is from)

1.3 Quality Criteria for Model Evaluation¶

We select two complementary metrics that reflect our business priorities:

Primary Metric: ROC-AUC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve)

ROC-AUC measures the model's ability to rank customers by default risk across all possible classification thresholds. This is essential because:

  • Our operational use case might require ranking customers by risk level, not just binary classification. ROC-AUC can provide that if we want to identify the riskiest 10%, 20%, or 30% of customers so that intervention contingent matches intervention capacity.
  • ROC-AUC is insensitive to class imbalance (78% non-default vs. 22% default -> see IDA chapter), unlike accuracy which would reward a naive "predict everyone as non-default" strategy.
  • It allows comparison across models without committing to a specific decision threshold prematurely.

Secondary Metric: F1-Score (Macro-Averaged)

F1-Macro averages the F1-score across both classes equally, providing a balanced view of performance on both defaulters and non-defaulters. We choose this because:

  • It penalizes models that achieve high performance on the majority class while neglecting the minority class (defaulters).
  • The harmonic mean nature of F1 requires reasonable performance on both precision and recall—we cannot afford to flag too many false positives (damaging customer relationships) nor miss too many true defaults (financial losses).
  • Macro-averaging ensures that our minority class (credit default) receives equal weight in evaluation despite its smaller size.

Why not Recall alone? While minimizing false negatives (missed defaults) is critical, optimizing purely for recall would flag excessive false positives, overwhelming our intervention capacity and potentially alienating good customers. F1-Macro enforces the necessary balance.

2.0 The Data¶

The dataset is the UCI Credit Card Default Dataset (https://archive-beta.ics.uci.edu/dataset/350/default+of+credit+card+clients), originally published by Yeh & Lien (2009) and collected from a major bank in Taiwan. It contains payment and billing information for 30,000 credit card customers observed from April to September 2005, with the target variable indicating whether each customer defaulted in October 2005. The dataset is published under the CC BY 4.0 license allowing for the sharing and adaptation of the dataset for any purpose, provided that the appropriate credit is given.

Why This Dataset?¶

This dataset is well-suited for our feasibility study because:

  1. Rich behavioral features: Six months of payment history, bill amounts, and repayment behavior—exactly the signals our legacy system fails to capture yet not too many features to be too complex as a starting point.

  2. Interpretable features: All variables have clear business meaning and are relatively well documented (we will see limitations to this statement soon). This emeaningfulness of the features enables direct model validation by domain experts and regulatory compliance.

  3. Sufficient sample size: 30,000 customers provide enough data for reliable cross-validation while remaining computationally manageable.

The statistical description alone already reveals valuable information about our credit customers. These insights (about demographics, etc.) are not just interesting for our company, but give away some implications that will lead our machine learning experiments.

Key observations:

Credit Limit (LIMIT_BAL):

  • Range from 10,000 to 1,000,000 NT dollars with high variability
  • Right-skewed distribution (mean > median)
  • ML implication: Large range would dominate KNN distance calculations → Scaling will be essential for KNN

Demographics:

  • SEX: Binary (1=male, 2=female, no other values), mean 1.6 indicates more female customers
  • AGE: 21-79 years, mean ~35 years
  • EDUCATION: Contains undocumented values. The documentation only defines the values 1-4. The values 0 and 6 (and possibly 5) seem to also be present.
  • MARRIAGE: Contains undocumented value 0 (documentation only defines 1-3)
  • ML implication: The undocumented values will make our analysis (or rather preprocessing) more complex since we need to one-hot-encode these categorical values for a thorough analyisis (exlanation see task 4). How exactly this is handled is discussed task 4.

Payment Status (PAY_0 to PAY_6):

  • Range -2 to 8 representing payment behavior (-2=no consumption, -1=paid duly, 0=revolving credit, 1-8=months delayed)
  • 75th percentile is 0 for all PAY variables → at least 75% of customers pay on time
  • ML implication: Likely the strongest predictors - past payment behavior is highly indicative of future default. As mentioned above the undocumented values 0 and -2 will need attention in task 4.

Bill Amounts (BILL_AMT1-6):

  • Contains negative values (min ~-340,000) representing overpayments/credits
  • High standard deviations indicate large variability
  • ML implication: Negative values may indicate responsible customers (less likely to default). High multicollinearity expected between months (redundant information, but acceptable for our algorithms)

Payment Amounts (PAY_AMT1-6):

  • All non-negative, highly right-skewed (mean >> median)
  • Extreme outliers (max ~1.7 million NT dollars)
  • ML implication: Decision Trees handle skewness well. KNN may be affected by outliers even after scaling, but we accept this limitation instead of removing data

4.0 EDA and Preprocessing¶

Our initial data analysis revealed a relatively clean dataset: no missing values, consistent datatypes, and 30,000 samples across 23 features. However, several preprocessing steps are required before model training. Alongside these Preprocessing steps we will

  1. Handling undocumented categorical values: The features EDUCATION and MARRIAGE contain values (0, 5, 6) not defined in the official documentation. We will investigate these and map them appropriately.

  2. Encoding nominal features: SEX, EDUCATION, and MARRIAGE are nominal categories without inherent order. One-hot encoding will prevent our algorithms from inferring false ordinal relationships.

  3. Transforming payment status features: The PAY_X variables mix ordinal delay information (1-8 months) with categorical payment behaviors (-2, -1, 0). We will separate these semantically distinct components to improve model performance—particularly for KNN, which relies on meaningful distance calculations.

After preprocessing, we examine feature distributions and correlations with the target variable to further inform our modeling strategy.

4.1 Handling undocumented categorical values¶

The dataset documentation defines EDUCATION values 1-4 (graduate school, university, high school, others) and MARRIAGE values 1-3 (married, single, others). However, our data contains undocumented values: EDUCATION includes 0, 5, and 6, while MARRIAGE includes 0.

Since both features have an "others" category (EDUCATION=4, MARRIAGE=3), we consolidate the undocumented values into these existing categories. This preserves all samples while maintaining interpretable feature values.

To verify this consolidation does not distort our data, we compare the target distribution within the "others" category before and after reassignment. A significant shift would indicate that the undocumented values represent a distinct subpopulation—in which case, alternative handling might be warranted.

Reflection: The reassignment has minimal impact on the dataset for two reasons. First, the undocumented values are rare—even after consolidation, the "others" category remains more than 10 times smaller than the next largest group (high school). Second, the target distribution within "others" shifted only slightly (EDUCATION: 5.7% → 7.1% default rate; MARRIAGE: 26.0% → 23.6%), indicating that the undocumented values do not represent a fundamentally different population.

One caveat: We cannot rule out that specific undocumented codes (e.g., EDUCATION=0) might have carried distinct predictive signal. However, with only 14 to 280 samples per code, any patterns would be statistically unreliable and difficult to interpret in a business context. Consolidating these values prioritizes model stability over speculative gains from tiny subgroups.

4.2 One-Hot Encoding Nominal Features¶

The features SEX, EDUCATION, and MARRIAGE are nominal categories with no inherent order. Retaining their integer encoding (e.g., EDUCATION: 1, 2, 3, 4) would introduce spurious ordinal relationships—implying, for instance, that "university" (2) lies between "graduate school" (1) and "high school" (3), or that the distance between categories is uniform and meaningful.

This matters particularly for KNN, which computes distances between samples. With integer encoding, a graduate school customer (EDUCATION=1) would appear "closer" to a university customer (EDUCATION=2) than to someone with "other" education (EDUCATION=4)—a meaningless distinction that could bias neighbor selection.

One-hot encoding resolves this by creating binary indicator columns for each category. All categories become equidistant in feature space, allowing both KNN and Decision Trees to treat them as independent groups without imposed hierarchy.

4.3 Transforming Payment Status Features¶

The PAY_X features (PAY_0 through PAY_6) encode repayment status for each of the six months prior to the prediction window. As this subchapter will show, these are our most predictive features. This makes sense intuitively: past payment behavior strongly signals future default risk. However, the encoding mixes two different types of information:

Ordinal component (1-8): Number of months payment is delayed. Here, distances are meaningful—a 3-month delay is worse than a 1-month delay, and the progression is linear.

Categorical component (-2, -1, 0): The dataset documentation only defines -1 as "paid in full." The meanings of -2 and 0 are not documented. What we can observe is that all three values represent states distinct from active payment delay—but crucially, they have no natural ordering among themselves. There is no reason to assume -2 < -1 < 0 represents a meaningful progression, yet the integer encoding implies exactly this, which would distort KNN's distance calculations.

Our approach: Rather than assuming what -2 and 0 represent, we treat each as a distinct categorical state:

  1. Creating binary indicator features (PAY_X_-2, PAY_X_paid_duly(-1), PAY_X_0) for each of the three non-delay values
  2. Transforming the original PAY_X to a clean ordinal scale: values ≤ 0 become 0 (not delayed), while values 1-8 remain unchanged (months delayed)

This adds 18 binary features (3 indicators × 6 months) but preserves all information without making assumptions about undocumented values. The model can learn whether -2 and 0 carry predictive signal, even if we cannot interpret their business meaning. Decision Trees can now split directly on these specific states, while KNN benefits from semantically meaningful distances in the ordinal delay component.

### PAY feature transformation

# Create list of columns to transform to iterate over
pay_cols = ['PAY_0', 'PAY_2', 'PAY_3', 'PAY_4', 'PAY_5', 'PAY_6']

# Iterate over columns and execute described changes
for col in pay_cols:
    # Create binary indicator features
    df[f'{col}_-2'] = (df[col] == -2).astype(int)
    df[f'{col}_paid_duly(-1)'] = (df[col] == -1).astype(int)
    df[f'{col}_0'] = (df[col] == 0).astype(int)
    
    # Transform original: map -2, -1, 0 → 0 (not delayed)
    df[col] = df[col].apply(lambda x: 0 if x <= 0 else x)

print(f"New feature count: {df.shape[1]} (was 24, added 6*3=18 binary features)")

Reflection: The correlation matrix confirms that our transformation improved feature quality. The positive correlation between PAY_X (now representing only delay months) and the target variable increased after removing the ambiguous negative values. The ordinal delay component now carries a cleaner signal: higher values consistently indicate higher default risk.

The binary indicator features (-2, _paid_duly, 0) all show slight negative correlations with default. Without assuming what -2 and 0 specifically mean, we can observe empirically that these non-delay states are associated with lower default probability—useful predictive signal that would have been obscured in the original mixed encoding.

The correlation matrix also reveals temporal autocorrelation typical of behavioral time series: diagonal bands of high correlation indicate that payment behavior persists across months. A customer who paid late in August likely paid late in July as well. This explains why PAY_0 (most recent month) shows the strongest correlation with default (0.40), while earlier months show progressively weaker correlations (PAY_6: 0.24). Recent behavior is simply more predictive of near-future behavior.

4.4 Credit Limit (LIMIT_BAL): Skewed Distribution and Correlation with Default Risk¶

Credit limit is the single continuous feature in our dataset that reflects our bank's prior risk assessment of each customer. Unlike payment history (which captures customer behavior), LIMIT_BAL represents a value the experts at our bank set—banks typically assign higher limits to customers they deem lower risk based on income, credit history, and other factors at account opening.

This makes LIMIT_BAL particularly interesting: if lower credit limits correlate with higher default rates, it may indicate either (a) that the bank's original risk assessment has predictive validity, or (b) that customers with lower limits face tighter financial constraints that increase default probability.

We examine the distribution separated by default status to assess whether credit limit carries predictive signal independent of payment behavior, and to understand the skewness identified in our descriptive statistics—which has implications for feature scaling in KNN.

LIMIT_BAL Statistics:
  Mean:        167,484 NT$
  Median:      140,000 NT$
  Skew:           0.99 (positive = right-skewed)

Observations:

The distribution is right-skewed (skewness = 0.99), with most customers having credit limits below 200,000 NT$ while a long tail extends up to 1,000,000 NT$. The mean (167,484 NT$) exceeds the median (140,000 NT$), confirming the skewness.

Comparing default vs. non-default customers reveals an important pattern: defaulters (orange) are more concentrated at lower credit limits, with their distribution peaking around 50,000 NT$. Non-defaulters (blue) show a broader distribution extending to higher credit limits. The boxplot confirms this—defaulters have a lower median credit limit and fewer high-value outliers.

This suggests that lower credit limits correlate with higher default risk. We can therefore expect it to play an imprtant role in our predictions beside the behavioural features.

ML Implications: The skewness affects our algorithms differently. KNN relies on distance calculations, and StandardScaler—which uses mean and standard deviation—is sensitive to outliers. After scaling, most values cluster tightly while outliers create extreme distances that can dominate neighbor selection. RobustScaler, which uses median and interquartile range, would mitigate this issue. Decision Trees are unaffected by skewness since they simply find optimal split thresholds (e.g., LIMIT_BAL > 150,000) regardless of distribution shape.

5.0 First Impressions¶

5.1: Default Setup with Baseline, KNN and Decision Tree (anpassen)¶

Baseline (B): We use a stratified random classifier that predicts class labels according to the training set's class distribution. This represents the performance we would expect from random guessing while respecting class imbalance—any useful model must substantially outperform this baseline.

Algorithm A1 - K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN): A distance-based algorithm that classifies samples based on the majority class among their k nearest neighbors.

Preprocessing requirements:

  • Feature scaling is essential. KNN computes Euclidean distances, so features with larger ranges (e.g., LIMIT_BAL: 10,000-1,000,000) would dominate features with smaller ranges (e.g., AGE: 21-79). We apply RobustScaler to scale the data while taking into account that outliers might distort scaling with methods like standard scaler.
  • Our one-hot encoded and binary indicator features are already on a 0/1 scale, but scaling ensures consistency across all features.

Algorithm A2 - Decision Tree: A rule-based algorithm that recursively partitions the feature space using threshold-based splits.

Preprocessing requirements:

  • No scaling required. Decision Trees are invariant to monotonic transformations of features since they only consider relative ordering for split decisions.
  • One-hot encoding (already applied) allows the tree to split on individual categories rather than arbitrary numeric thresholds.
In [19]:
### Train-test split (80/20, stratified to preserve class distribution)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, 
    test_size=0.2, 
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE, 
    stratify=y
)

print(f"Training set: {X_train.shape[0]} samples")
print(f"Test set:     {X_test.shape[0]} samples")
print(f"Class distribution preserved: {y_test.mean():.1%} default rate in test set")

### Fitting algorithms and baseline

# --- Baseline: Stratified Random Classifier ---
baseline = DummyClassifier(strategy='stratified', random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
baseline.fit(X_train, y_train)

# --- KNN: With feature scaling ---
scaler = RobustScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)

knn = KNeighborsClassifier()  # default: n_neighbors=5, weights='uniform'
knn.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

# --- Decision Tree: No scaling needed ---
dt = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE)  # default: no max_depth
dt.fit(X_train, y_train)

min_samples_split samples. 		None

The minimum number of samples required to split an internal node:

The minimum number of samples required to be at a leaf node.

The number of features to consider when looking for the best split:

- If int, then consider `max_features` features at each split.
- If float, then `max_features` is a fraction and
`max(1, int(max_features * n_features_in_))` features are considered at
each split.
- If "sqrt", then `max_features=sqrt(n_features)`.
- If "log2", then `max_features=log2(n_features)`.
- If None, then `max_features=n_features`.

.. note::

The search for a split does not stop until at least one
valid partition of the node samples is found, even if it requires to
effectively inspect more than ``max_features`` features. 		None
random_state random_state: int, RandomState instance or None, default=None

Controls the randomness of the estimator. The features are always
randomly permuted at each split, even if ``splitter`` is set to
``"best"``. When ``max_features < n_features``, the algorithm will
select ``max_features`` at random at each split before finding the best
split among them. But the best found split may vary across different
runs, even if ``max_features=n_features``. That is the case, if the
improvement of the criterion is identical for several splits and one
split has to be selected at random. To obtain a deterministic behaviour
during fitting, ``random_state`` has to be fixed to an integer.
See :term:`Glossary ` for details. 		42
max_leaf_nodes max_leaf_nodes: int, default=None

Grow a tree with ``max_leaf_nodes`` in best-first fashion.
Best nodes are defined as relative reduction in impurity.
If None then unlimited number of leaf nodes. 		None
min_impurity_decrease min_impurity_decrease: float, default=0.0

A node will be split if this split induces a decrease of the impurity
greater than or equal to this value.

The weighted impurity decrease equation is the following::

N_t / N * (impurity - N_t_R / N_t * right_impurity
- N_t_L / N_t * left_impurity)

where ``N`` is the total number of samples, ``N_t`` is the number of
samples at the current node, ``N_t_L`` is the number of samples in the
left child, and ``N_t_R`` is the number of samples in the right child.

``N``, ``N_t``, ``N_t_R`` and ``N_t_L`` all refer to the weighted sum,
if ``sample_weight`` is passed.

.. versionadded:: 0.19 		0.0
class_weight class_weight: dict, list of dict or "balanced", default=None

Weights associated with classes in the form ``{class_label: weight}``.
If None, all classes are supposed to have weight one. For
multi-output problems, a list of dicts can be provided in the same
order as the columns of y.

Note that for multioutput (including multilabel) weights should be
defined for each class of every column in its own dict. For example,
for four-class multilabel classification weights should be
[{0: 1, 1: 1}, {0: 1, 1: 5}, {0: 1, 1: 1}, {0: 1, 1: 1}] instead of
[{1:1}, {2:5}, {3:1}, {4:1}].

The "balanced" mode uses the values of y to automatically adjust
weights inversely proportional to class frequencies in the input data
as ``n_samples / (n_classes * np.bincount(y))``

For multi-output, the weights of each column of y will be multiplied.

Note that these weights will be multiplied with sample_weight (passed
through the fit method) if sample_weight is specified. 		None
ccp_alpha ccp_alpha: non-negative float, default=0.0

Complexity parameter used for Minimal Cost-Complexity Pruning. The
subtree with the largest cost complexity that is smaller than
``ccp_alpha`` will be chosen. By default, no pruning is performed. See
:ref:`minimal_cost_complexity_pruning` for details. See
:ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_tree_plot_cost_complexity_pruning.py`

.. versionadded:: 0.22 		0.0
monotonic_cst monotonic_cst: array-like of int of shape (n_features), default=None

Indicates the monotonicity constraint to enforce on each feature.
- 1: monotonic increase
- 0: no constraint
- -1: monotonic decrease

If monotonic_cst is None, no constraints are applied.

Monotonicity constraints are not supported for:
- multiclass classifications (i.e. when `n_classes > 2`),
- multioutput classifications (i.e. when `n_outputs_ > 1`),
- classifications trained on data with missing values.

The constraints hold over the probability of the positive class.

### 5.4 Evaluation on the test set and comparison in table

def evaluate_model(model, X_test, y_test, model_name):
    """Evaluate model and return metrics dictionary."""
    y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
    y_proba = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    
    return {
        'Model': model_name,
        'ROC-AUC': roc_auc_score(y_test, y_proba),
        'F1-Macro': f1_score(y_test, y_pred, average='macro')
    }

# Evaluate all models (note: KNN uses scaled test data)
results = pd.DataFrame([
    evaluate_model(baseline, X_test, y_test, 'Baseline (Stratified)'),
    evaluate_model(knn, X_test_scaled, y_test, 'KNN (default)'),
    evaluate_model(dt, X_test, y_test, 'Decision Tree (default)')
])

# The Decision Tree is likely overfitting in default mode so we print these statistics to confirm
print(f"\nDecision Tree Statistics:")
print(f"  Total nodes: {dt.tree_.node_count}")
print(f"  Max depth: {dt.get_depth()}")
print(f"  Number of leaves: {dt.get_n_leaves()}")

2 Decision Tree (default) 0.603626 0.600228

About the Metrics: ROC-AUC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve) measures a model's ability to rank positive cases (defaulters) higher than negative cases (non-defaulters) across all classification thresholds. A score of 0.5 indicates random ranking—no better than guessing—while 1.0 represents perfect separation. F1-Macro is the unweighted average of F1-scores for both classes, where F1 itself is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. This metric penalizes models that perform well on one class while neglecting the other.

Baseline (Stratified): Both metrics hover around 0.50, confirming that random guessing according to class distribution provides no predictive value. This establishes our lower bound—any useful model must substantially exceed these scores.

KNN (default, k=5): With ROC-AUC of 0.71, KNN demonstrates meaningful predictive ability. A score of 0.71 means that when we randomly select one defaulter and one non-defaulter, KNN ranks the defaulter as higher risk 70% of the time. The F1-Macro of 0.65 indicates reasonable balance between precision and recall across both classes, though there is room for improvement.

Decision Tree (default, unlimited depth): The lower scores (ROC-AUC: 0.6, F1-Macro: 0.6) are very certainly due to overfitting. Without depth constraints, the tree memorizes training data patterns that do not generalize to unseen data. The gap between Decision Tree and KNN performance should narrow—or even reverse—after hyperparameter tuning in Task 6, where limiting tree depth will improve generalization.

Key Takeaway: Both algorithms substantially outperform the baseline, confirming that our preprocessed features contain predictive signal for credit default. However, these results are based on a single train-test split and may vary with different random partitions. Cross-validation will provide more robust estimates.

Stability: The standard deviations from cross-validation reveal how sensitive each model is to different data splits. All three models show remarkably low variance (std ≤ 0.01 (except KNN ROC-AUC)), indicating highly stable performance across folds. This confirms that our dataset of 30,000 samples is large enough that different 80/20 partitions yield consistent results. The single-split results closely match the CV means—our initial evaluation was representative, not an artifact of a lucky partition.

Quality: Cross-validation confirms the ranking observed in the single split: KNN (ROC-AUC: 0.703) outperforms Decision Tree (ROC-AUC: 0.605), and both substantially exceed the baseline (ROC-AUC: 0.495). With KNN achieving 0.703, the model correctly ranks a randomly selected defaulter above a randomly selected non-defaulter 70% of the time—a meaningful improvement over the 50% baseline.

Overfitting: The Decision Tree's weaker generalization despite its ability to perfectly memorize training data signals overfitting. With unlimited depth, the tree learns noise and sample-specific patterns that do not transfer to unseen data. KNN's implicit regularization—averaging over k=5 neighbors—provides natural smoothing that can prevent overfitting to individual training points to an extend. While KNN exhibits substantially better generalization than the unrestricted Decision Tree (better scores), the learning curve reveals a persistent gap between training and validation performance that does not close with increasing training set size (see code cell below). This indicates that KNN is also variance-dominated in its default configuration resulting in overfitting albeit to a lesser extent.

Conclusion: Both algorithms demonstrate genuine predictive ability for credit default, with KNN currently leading by a margin of approximately 0.09 ROC-AUC. However, default hyperparameters rarely represent optimal configurations. The nested cross-validation in Task 6 will tune hyperparameters—particularly constraining Decision Tree depth—and determine whether the performance gap narrows or reverses.

Note on data leakage:
For this exploratory analysis, feature scaling for KNN was performed globally before cross-validation, which introduces mild data leakage during CV. Given the large dataset and the use of robust scaling, the resulting bias is expected to be negligible. This simplification was intentionally accepted to keep the initial performance assessment clear and focused; all final model selection and evaluation steps use leakage-free pipelines.

6.0 Hyperparameter Optimization – Nested Cross Validation¶

In Task 5, we evaluated algorithms with default hyperparameters. Now we use nested cross-validation to find optimal hyperparameters while maintaining unbiased performance estimates. The outer loop evaluates generalization performance, while the inner loop tunes hyperparameters via grid search.

6.1 Setup Hyperparameter Grid and Pipeline¶

Before running nested CV, we define the search space for each algorithm. The hyperparameter grids are designed to explore the most impactful parameters while keeping computational cost manageable.

KNN Hyperparameters:

  • n_neighbors: Controls model complexity. Fewer neighbors = more flexible but prone to noise; more neighbors = smoother but may miss local patterns.
  • weights: 'uniform' treats all neighbors equally; 'distance' weights closer neighbors more heavily.
  • metric: Distance measure affects which points are considered "neighbors."

Decision Tree Hyperparameters:

  • max_depth: Primary regularization parameter. Limits tree complexity to prevent overfitting—critical given our Task 5 observation that unlimited depth leads to memorization.
  • min_samples_split: Minimum samples required to split a node. Higher values create simpler trees.
  • criterion: Split quality measure. 'gini' and 'entropy' often yield similar results but can differ on specific datasets.
In [25]:
# CV Configuration for inner loop
NUM_INNER_SPLITS = 5  # Inner CV for hyperparameter tuning
NUM_INNER_REPEATS = 2 # Inner CV repeats for stable hyperparam selection

# Hyperparameter grids
param_grid_knn = {
    'estimator__n_neighbors': [3, 5, 7, 11, 15],
    'estimator__weights': ['uniform', 'distance'],
    'estimator__metric': ['euclidean', 'manhattan']
}

param_grid_dt = {
    'estimator__max_depth': [3, 5, 7, 10, 15, None],
    'estimator__min_samples_split': [2, 5, 10, 20],
    'estimator__criterion': ['gini', 'entropy']
}

print(f"KNN grid: {5*2*2} = 20 combinations")
print(f"Decision Tree grid: {6*4*2} = 48 combinations")

KNN grid: 20 = 20 combinations
Decision Tree grid: 48 = 48 combinations

Total grid search effort: 20 + 48 = 68 hyperparameter combinations, each evaluated with 10 inner CV folds (5 splits × 2 repeats), resulting in 680 model fits per outer fold.

In [26]:
### Setting up Pipeline function with an optional scaling for the KNN estimators

def get_pipeline(estimator, scale=False):
    """
    Create a pipeline with optional scaling.
    
    Parameters:
    -----------
    estimator : sklearn estimator
        The classifier to use
    scale : bool
        Whether to include RobustScaler (needed for distance-based algorithms like KNN)
    
    Returns:
    --------
    Pipeline : sklearn Pipeline object
    """
    if scale:
        return Pipeline([
            ('scaler', RobustScaler()),
            ('estimator', estimator)
        ])
    else:
        return Pipeline([
            ('estimator', estimator)
        ])

6.2 Setup and run Nested Cross-Validation¶

We now execute the nested CV procedure for all three model types:

  1. Baseline: No hyperparameters to tune, this serves as lower bound reference
  2. KNN: With RobustScaler in pipeline and hyperparameter tuning
  3. Decision Tree: Without scaling, with hyperparameter tuning

The outer loop uses the same 10-fold stratified CV from Task 5 for comparability. The inner loop uses repeated stratified CV (5 folds × 2 repeats) to provide stable hyperparameter selection despite the reduced sample size in each outer training fold.

In [27]:
### Nested CV Setup

def nested_cv(pipeline, param_grid, X, y, name):
    """
    Run nested cross-validation with GridSearch hyperparameter tuning.
    
    Outer CV: Unbiased performance estimation
    Inner CV: Hyperparameter tuning via GridSearchCV
    """
    print(f"\n{name}:")

    # Our Bank clearly prefers performance over time efficiency, but while working on the experiments we are interested in seeing training times
    start = time.time()
    
    # Outer CV strategy (reusing cv from task 5)
    outer_cv = cv
    
    # Inner CV strategy
    inner_cv = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(
        n_splits=NUM_INNER_SPLITS,    # 5 folds
        n_repeats=NUM_INNER_REPEATS,  # 2 repeats, inuitively this makes more sense for outer loop but exercise states outer loop should stay as in task 5
        random_state=RANDOM_STATE
    )
    
    # GridSearchCV handles inner loop
    grid_search = GridSearchCV(
        estimator=pipeline,
        param_grid=param_grid,
        cv=inner_cv,
        scoring='roc_auc',
        refit=True,
        n_jobs=1 # While working on the notebook this was -1 (all available cores) but to ensure consistent results across different environments I set it to 1
    )
    
    # cross_validate handles outer loop
    cv_results = cross_validate(
        grid_search, X, y,
        cv=outer_cv,
        scoring={'roc_auc': 'roc_auc', 'f1_macro': 'f1_macro'},
        return_estimator=True,
        n_jobs=1
    )
    
    elapsed = time.time() - start
    
    # Extract results
    roc_auc_scores = cv_results['test_roc_auc']
    f1_scores = cv_results['test_f1_macro']
    
    print(f"  ROC-AUC: {roc_auc_scores.mean():.4f} ± {roc_auc_scores.std():.4f}")
    print(f"  F1-Macro: {f1_scores.mean():.4f} ± {f1_scores.std():.4f}")
    print(f"  Time: {elapsed:.1f}s")
    
    return {
        'name': name,
        'roc_auc_mean': roc_auc_scores.mean(),
        'roc_auc_std': roc_auc_scores.std(),
        'f1_mean': f1_scores.mean(),
        'f1_std': f1_scores.std(),
        'cv_results': cv_results
    }
In [28]:

    {},  # Empty grid
    X, y,

)

    param_grid_knn,

    "KNN"
)

# Decision Tree with hyperparameter tuning (no scaling needed)
dt_results = nested_cv(
    get_pipeline(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE), scale=False),
    param_grid_dt,
    X, y,
    "Decision Tree"
)

6.4 Final Model Selection and Training on final algorythm¶

Based on nested CV results, we select the best-performing (Decision Tree) algorithm and train the final model M on the complete dataset. This final model will be:

  1. Used for deployment in the credit risk assessment system
  2. Used for visualizing the Decision Tree in the following subchapter
  3. Analyzed for feature importance in Task 7
  4. The basis for business recommendations in Task 8

We perform one final GridSearchCV on all data to determine the optimal hyperparameters for the full dataset. The nested CV score from 6.2 remains our unbiased performance estimate—the final training simply produces the deployable model.

The Decision Tree with max_depth=7, min_samples_split=20, and criterion='entropy' emerges as our final model M. This configuration balances:

  • Complexity control: Depth 7 allows capturing payment behavior patterns without memorizing individual customers
  • Statistical reliability: Requiring 20 samples per split ensures decisions are based on sufficient evidence
  • Information-theoretic splits: Entropy criterion maximizes information gain at each decision point

The CV score on full data (0.758) closely matches our nested CV estimate (0.756), confirming that our performance expectations are realistic and not artifacts of particular data splits.

7.0 Feature Importance / Feature Ablation Study¶

With our final model M selected and trained, we now investigate which features drive predictions. We use permutation importance—a model-agnostic method that measures how much performance degrades when a feature's relationship with the target is destroyed by random shuffling.

7.1 Compute and Visualize Feature Importance¶

Why Permutation Importance?

While Decision Trees provide built-in feature importance (based on impurity reduction), permutation importance offers several advantages:

  • Model-agnostic: Same method works for any algorithm, enabling fair comparison
  • Accounts for feature interactions: Measures importance in context of other features
  • Intuitive interpretation: "How much does performance drop if this feature becomes noise?"

Since it was not discussed in the lecture this is a brief overview of the methodoly:

  1. Compute baseline performance on original data
  2. For each feature:
    • Randomly shuffle that feature's values (breaking its relationship with target)
    • Measure new performance
    • Importance = baseline performance − shuffled performance
  3. Repeat multiple times (n_repeats=30) for stable estimates

A high importance score means the model heavily relies on that feature; zero or negative importance means the feature is uninformative or even harmful.

In [37]:
### Compute feature importance using permutation importance

# Use final_model_M from Task 6 (already trained on full dataset)
print(f"Using final_model_M: {type(final_model_M.named_steps['estimator']).__name__}")

# Compute permutation importance
# n_repeats: Number of times to permute each feature (more = stable estimates)
# scoring: Metric to measure performance drop
perm_importance = permutation_importance(
    final_model_M, X, y,
    n_repeats=30,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    scoring='roc_auc',
    n_jobs=1
)

# Create DataFrame with results
feature_importance_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'Feature': X.columns,
    'Importance Mean': perm_importance.importances_mean,
    'Importance Std': perm_importance.importances_std
}).sort_values('Importance Mean', ascending=False)

Feature Importance Insights:

The permutation importance reveals a clear hierarchy with a long-tail distribution:

Top Predictors (Importance > 0.01):

  • Payment status features (PAY_0, PAY_2, PAY_3) dominate—recent payment behavior is the strongest default signal
  • BILL_AMT1 and LIMIT_BAL provide secondary predictive power
  • PAY_AMT features (actual payment amounts) contribute meaningful signal

Temporal Pattern: Recent months have the tendency to matter more than older months (E.g. PAY_0 (September) has ~3x the importance of PAY_6 (April))

Zero-Importance Features: Many of our engineered binary features show zero importance. This doesn't mean they're inherently useless—the Decision Tree may simply not have selected them given the presence of stronger alternatives and the max_depth constraint.

Key Finding: The top 5 features (PAY_0, BILL_AMT1, PAY_2, LIMIT_BAL, PAY_AMT3) account for the majority of predictive signal. This concentration suggests a simpler model with fewer features might achieve comparable performance.

7.2 Ablation Study¶

The task decription only states to perform an ablation study with the two least important features. The Decision Tree however resulted in 22 features with 0 importance that are not used in the Decision Tree at all. I therefore decided to include used features in the ablation study. We now empirically assess how sensitive the final Decision Tree model is to the removal of features with low or zero estimated importance. Building on the permutation importance analysis, the ablation study evaluates whether such features meaningfully contribute to predictive performance or can be removed without degradation.

To this end, we compare multiple ablation configurations that progressively remove different groups of features:

Configuration Features Removed Purpose
Full Model None Baseline performance
Without F1 Second least important feature Test impact of a low-importance feature
Without F2 Least important feature Test impact of a near-zero-importance feature
Without F1 & F2 Both Test combined removal of lowest-ranked features
Without UNUSED All features unused by the final tree Test redundancy of features not selected in any split
Without U1 / U2 One low-importance used feature Test importance among features actively used by the model
Without U1 & U2 Two lowest-importance used features Test cumulative effect on model performance
Without UNUSED + U1/U2 Combination of unused and weakly used features Test robustness under more aggressive feature removal

Here, unused features are those that do not appear in any split of the trained Decision Tree, while used features correspond to features actively selected by the model but exhibiting low permutation importance.

Methodology:

  • The same hyperparameters as the final optimized model (Model M) are used throughout.
  • For each configuration, the specified features are removed prior to training.
  • Performance is evaluated using stratified cross-validation with the same CV strategy as in Task 6.
  • ROC-AUC and F1-Macro are reported as mean ± standard deviation.

Expected Outcome: If the permutation importance estimates are reliable, removing features with zero or near-zero importance—particularly those unused by the tree—should result in little to no performance degradation. In contrast, removing weakly important but actively used features may lead to small but measurable declines, providing insight into redundancy, robustness, and the model’s reliance on specific predictors.

In [39]:
### Perform Ablation Study
# - remove the two least important features
# - remove all features unused by the final tree (no splits)
# - remove the two least important *used* features (appear in tree)
# - and combinations (used-low, unused-all, both)

# --- CV strategy for ablation ---
cv_ablation = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

def create_feature_dropper(features_to_drop):
    """Create a transformer that drops specified features."""
    def drop_features(X):
        if isinstance(X, pd.DataFrame):
            return X.drop(columns=features_to_drop, errors='ignore')
        return X
    return FunctionTransformer(drop_features, validate=False)

def run_ablation_cv(X, y, features_to_drop, cv):
    """Run cross-validation with specified features removed."""
    pipeline = Pipeline([
        ('dropper', create_feature_dropper(features_to_drop)),
        ('estimator', DecisionTreeClassifier(
            max_depth=final_hyperparameters['estimator__max_depth'],
            min_samples_split=final_hyperparameters['estimator__min_samples_split'],
            criterion=final_hyperparameters['estimator__criterion'],
            random_state=RANDOM_STATE
        ))
    ])

    roc_auc_scores = cross_val_score(pipeline, X, y, cv=cv, scoring='roc_auc')
    f1_scores = cross_val_score(pipeline, X, y, cv=cv, scoring='f1_macro')

    return {
        'roc_auc_mean': roc_auc_scores.mean(),
        'roc_auc_std': roc_auc_scores.std(),
        'f1_mean': f1_scores.mean(),
        'f1_std': f1_scores.std()
    }

# Identify (A) unused-by-tree features and (B) lowest-used features

# Final trained model on full data (Task 6)
final_tree = final_model_M.named_steps['estimator']
feature_names = list(X.columns)

# Features actually used in splits (tree feature indices >= 0)
used_feature_idx = set(final_tree.tree_.feature[final_tree.tree_.feature >= 0])
used_features = [feature_names[i] for i in sorted(used_feature_idx)]
unused_features = [f for f in feature_names if f not in used_features]

# Two least important features overall (same as before)
least_important = feature_importance_df.tail(2)
F1 = least_important.iloc[0]['Feature']  # second least important overall
F2 = least_important.iloc[1]['Feature']  # least important overall

# Two least important features among those actually used by the tree (based on permutation importance)
used_importance_df = feature_importance_df[feature_importance_df['Feature'].isin(used_features)].copy()
least_used_two = used_importance_df.sort_values('Importance Mean', ascending=True).head(2)

U1 = least_used_two.iloc[0]['Feature']  # least important among used
U2 = least_used_two.iloc[1]['Feature']  # second least important among used

print("Ablation targets:")
print(f"  Two least important overall:      F1={F1}, F2={F2}")
print(f"  Unused by final tree (count):     {len(unused_features)}")
print(f"  Two least important USED features: U1={U1}, U2={U2}")

The ablation study provides strong empirical support for the permutation importance analysis and offers additional insight into model robustness and redundancy.

Key Results:

  • Removing the two least important features (F1, F2), individually or jointly, results in no performance degradation. All observed changes in ROC-AUC (+0.0003 to +0.0005) and F1-Macro (+0.0022 to +0.0024) lie well within the cross-validation standard deviation.
  • Removing all features unused by the final tree (reducing the feature set from 47 to 25) leads to a slight performance improvement (Δ ROC-AUC ≈ +0.0015, Δ F1-Macro ≈ +0.0028), suggesting that these features were entirely redundant or mildly noisy.
  • Removing the two least important used features (U1, U2), either individually or together, again results in no measurable performance loss, and in some cases small positive deltas.
  • The most aggressive configurations—removing all unused features together with one or both weakly used features (23–24 features remaining)—achieve the best average performance observed (Δ ROC-AUC up to +0.0023, Δ F1-Macro up to +0.0039), while remaining statistically indistinguishable from the full model.

Across all configurations, performance differences remain small relative to the standard deviations, indicating statistical equivalence between the full and reduced models.

Practical Implications:

  1. Substantial Feature Redundancy Confirmed:
    Nearly half of the original feature set can be removed without harming—and in some cases slightly improving—generalization performance. This confirms that the final Decision Tree relies on a relatively compact subset of informative predictors.

  2. Model Simplification Benefits:
    Reducing the feature set from 47 to roughly 23–25 features would:

    • Lower model complexity and variance
    • Reduce data preprocessing and collection requirements
    • Simplify model interpretation and documentation, which is particularly valuable in regulated domains such as credit risk modeling

  3. Permutation Importance Validated:
    The close agreement between permutation importance rankings and ablation outcomes demonstrates that permutation importance provides a reliable estimate of feature relevance for this model. Features with zero or near-zero importance can be safely removed without adverse effects.

Recommendation:
For a production deployment, a reduced model trained on the subset of features with non-zero permutation importance—potentially combined with the exclusion of the weakest used features—offers a more parsimonious and interpretable alternative while maintaining equivalent predictive performance. The model performance with progressively more features dropped (top 5-6 important features significantly outperform other features in importance) should be investigated in the future.

8. Conclusions and Future Work¶

This project set out to evaluate the feasibility of applying interpretable machine learning methods to credit card default prediction using behavioral payment data. Across a structured experimental pipeline—including exploratory analysis, model comparison, learning curves, nested cross-validation, feature importance analysis, and ablation studies—we arrive at a set of technically sound and practically relevant conclusions.

8.1 Summary of Results¶

Model ROC-AUC (Default) ROC-AUC (Tuned) Δ ROC-AUC F1-Macro (Default) F1-Macro (Tuned)
Baseline ≈ 0.50 ≈ 0.50 +0.000 ≈ 0.50 ≈ 0.50
KNN ≈ 0.71 ≈ 0.74 +0.03 ≈ 0.65 ≈ 0.67
Decision Tree ≈ 0.62 ≈ 0.76 +0.14 ≈ 0.61 ≈ 0.68

We evaluated two interpretable machine learning algorithms—K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) and Decision Trees—on the UCI Credit Card Default dataset comprising 30,000 customers. Model performance was assessed using ROC-AUC as the primary metric and F1-Macro as a secondary metric to account for class imbalance.

Initial evaluations with default hyperparameters showed KNN outperforming an unconstrained Decision Tree. However, learning curve analysis revealed a persistent gap between training and validation performance for KNN, indicating variance-dominated behavior and mild overfitting that did not diminish with increasing training set size.

Hyperparameter optimization via nested cross-validation proved critical. In particular, constraining the maximum depth of the Decision Tree dramatically reduced overfitting and improved generalization performance. The optimized Decision Tree achieved a cross-validated ROC-AUC of approximately 0.756, outperforming KNN while retaining full interpretability.

Feature importance analysis further showed that predictive power is concentrated in a small subset of recent behavioral variables, with many features contributing little or no additional information. This finding was empirically confirmed through an ablation study, which demonstrated that removing low-importance or unused features does not degrade—and in some cases slightly improves—model performance.

Overall, these results demonstrate that interpretable models can extract meaningful predictive signal from behavioral payment data, that careful regularization is essential for reliable generalization, and that substantial feature redundancy can be eliminated without sacrificing performance.

8.2 Business Value Assessment¶

From a business perspective, the final Decision Tree model offers tangible value for credit risk management.

With an ROC-AUC of approximately 0.756, the model significantly improves upon random selection when ranking customers by default risk. In practical terms, if the institution were to flag the top 30% highest-risk customers for further review or intervention, the model would be expected to capture approximately 55–60% of actual defaulters, representing a respectable efficiency gain over the legacy system. The model should however be improved with newer data in future studies that explore this risk assessment method (see next subchapter).

Beyond predictive performance, interpretability is a central advantage. The Decision Tree provides transparent, rule-based explanations for each prediction, enabling credit analysts to understand, audit, and justify decisions. This is particularly important in regulated domains, where explainability and fairness are legal and ethical requirements.

Furthermore, the ablation study demonstrated that the model remains robust even when nearly half of the original features are removed. This indicates that the model relies on a compact, behaviorally meaningful subset of predictors, simplifying data requirements and reducing operational complexity.

8.3 Future Work¶

While the results are encouraging, several avenues for further improvement remain.

First, ensemble methods such as Random Forests or Gradient Boosting could be explored to assess whether additional performance gains are achievable while still retaining partial interpretability through feature importance analysis.

Second, threshold optimization based on asymmetric business costs would allow the model to be tailored to specific operational objectives, such as prioritizing the detection of defaulters over minimizing false positives.

Third, temporal validation should be incorporated. Training on earlier periods and testing on later periods would more closely reflect real-world deployment and provide a stricter estimate of generalization performance.

Finally, additional feature engineering—such as utilization ratios, payment trends, or aggregated behavioral indicators—may capture risk dynamics more effectively than raw monthly values. Removing all unsused features from the dataset might also make a second comparison study of KNN and Decision Tree worthwhile since KNN will likely perform better on fewer features.

8.4 Critical Reflection¶

Several methodological limitations should be acknowledged. Some preprocessing steps, such as feature encoding and early transformations, were applied globally during exploratory analysis. While these operations are deterministic and unlikely to leak label information, a fully production-ready pipeline would encapsulate all preprocessing steps within cross-validation folds to ensure complete isolation between training and evaluation data. This was partially addressed in later stages of the project through pipeline-based modeling and nested cross-validation (not for feature encoding).

Feature scaling for KNN was also performed globally during early diagnostic analyses, introducing mild data leakage. Given the large dataset size and the exploratory nature of these analyses, the impact is expected to be negligible and does not affect the overall conclusions. All final model evaluations were conducted using leakage-free procedures.

Finally, the dataset itself reflects consumer behavior from a specific historical and geographic context. Economic conditions, regulatory frameworks, and payment behavior have evolved since then. Any real-world deployment would therefore require retraining and validation on current data, as well as continuous monitoring to ensure stable performance over time.

Despite these limitations, the project demonstrates that interpretable machine learning models—when properly regularized and evaluated—can provide robust, transparent, and practically useful tools for credit default prediction.
